name: Colin Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. What you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start by loading the line truck at the electricity depot and checking the harness twice. I got my vocational certificate at 55 after years doing delivery work, so at 58 I'm the junior one asking where a fitting lives on the truck. I use an AI assistant each morning to quiz myself on equipment names, though I never let it tell me a line is dead. I like the crew and the outdoor work; the lower wage and the awkward climb down at the end are the hard bits.

say: I would call AI a **study partner** while insisting a meter and second worker check safety.
I would share my **equipment checklist** with the crew if it helps them.
think: I worry about **hotel shifts** and our thin savings even if AI changes little.
I know the assistant can name the **wrong connector** unless I check the manual.
do: Keep taking **line shifts** and quiz myself before the equipment assessment.
Transfer one **takeaway meal's cost** into an emergency account each payday.
feel: Steady on the truck, but embarrassed by our **small buffer** at home.
S0.quote: I can learn a new device quickly but still haven't built a spare month's rent.
fieldNote: Colin uses AI every morning, yet a **wrong connector size** keeps his safety judgment tied to physical checks.
His **money worry** predates AI and includes his wife's variable hotel hours as well as his lower line wage.

steps.text: Keep taking line shifts at the electricity company
Quiz himself on equipment names with AI and check answers against the printed manual
Transfer the cost of one Friday takeaway to an emergency account each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mates the AI assistant is a decent study partner, even if the big promises fizzle. The job still comes down to the test meter and another worker watching your hands. At the depot I'd probably show the younger crew the little checklist I made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Lena and I have less than a month's expenses saved. She cleans rooms at a small hotel, and her shifts can disappear when bookings are poor. If jobs and prices stay roughly as they are, I'm still trying to catch up after changing trades late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking line shifts and use the assistant to quiz me before the next equipment assessment. In the first year I'd keep checking every answer against our printed manual and ask the lead, Jo, when it disagrees. I'd also move the money from one takeaway meal each week into an emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel steady at work and a bit embarrassed at home. I can learn a new device quickly but still haven't built a spare month's rent. The ordinary bills are the frightening part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the assistant get wrong recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It called a connector by the wrong size last Tuesday. I held the real part next to the manual and saw the mismatch before we packed the truck. I told Jo because somebody less careful could have loaded it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save from the takeaway meal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena and I buy food on the way home every Friday when we're both worn out. We can cook a pot of rice and beans at home, then move that amount on payday. It's small, but it is money we don't already need for rent.

say: I would welcome **faster routing** only with enough time to isolate faults safely.
I would acknowledge that **planners and buyers** may lose tasks before line crews do.
think: I expect **speed targets** could hurt a junior worker still learning repairs.
I see gradual **field robots** as a later risk worth tracking.
do: Volunteer for the **tablet pilot** and record wrong pole locations or parts.
Practice **fault isolation** with Jo and apply for a maintenance trainee opening if available.
feel: Curious about the **new tablet**, yet anxious about a faster clock on each repair.
S1.quote: I'm also anxious that a faster work order will turn into a faster clock on the truck.
fieldNote: His curiosity yields a specific **error log**, rather than broad confidence that AI will improve every job.
The possible maintenance application reflects **past van repairs**, but he says he lacks formal training and needs paid shifts.

steps.text: Volunteer for the utility tablet pilot and log wrong locations or parts
Keep taking paid line shifts while any application is pending
Ask Jo for supervised fault-isolation practice
Apply for an internal vehicle-maintenance trainee opening if one appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that faster routing is useful if crews still get time to isolate a fault safely. The planners and buying staff may lose work first, and I wouldn't pretend our tablets create new posts for them. I would offer to test the work-order screen with the people who use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the company will count every saved minute and ask for more calls per shift. I'm still learning at the junior rate, so speed targets could expose me more than an experienced hand. The physical repair is there for now, but robots coming slowly still deserve watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the tablet pilot next month and keep a notebook of wrong locations or missing parts. In the first year I'd ask Jo for supervised fault-isolation practice and apply for the utility's vehicle-maintenance trainee post if it opens. I'd keep my line shifts while that application is pending; Lena's hotel wage cannot carry both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious enough to want the tablet in my hands. I'm also anxious that a faster work order will turn into a faster clock on the truck. Both feelings fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in that notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd note the pole number, what part the tablet said we needed, and what we actually used. One wrong location can waste half a morning, so a test only means something if we count the misses. I would show Jo the entries rather than post angry messages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why vehicle maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to repair delivery vans on weekends, but I've never had formal maintenance training. It's still hands-on and easier on a bad knee than climbing. There are few other line crews nearby, so a real internal opening matters.

say: I would ask for a **real timetable** for dispatch changes and later field robots.
I would tell colleagues that **2031 repair robots** could shrink the climbing crew.
think: I cannot rely on a **dispatch desk** after full thinking AI arrives.
I fear **lost shifts** because our savings cover less than a month.
do: Request a **paid maintenance apprenticeship** and apply to the bus garage now.
Keep **safe line shifts** in 2029 and seek wage support if hours fall.
feel: Alarmed about **immediate bills**, despite having applications to make.
S2.quote: My daily AI use won't make a junior lineworker irreplaceable, and a records job could go even sooner.
fieldNote: Colin refuses an easy **AI-savvy desk** narrative because full AGI threatens dispatch before robots reach field repairs.
He has an active **paid-work plan**, but neither a training place nor a garage offer is secured.

steps.text: Request a paid vehicle-maintenance apprenticeship from the utility
Apply for a hands-on position at the bus garage
Keep taking safe paid line shifts through 2029
Seek temporary wage support if line hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could run dispatch and stores before a robot touches the line. Around 2031, if robots do the repairs as well as us, the company will need far fewer climbers. I'd ask for a real timetable instead of a slogan about innovation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 60 when the office work changes and 63 when field robots arrive. My daily AI use won't make a junior lineworker irreplaceable, and a records job could go even sooner. With less than a month saved, I can't gamble on three unpaid years of study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request the company's paid vehicle-maintenance apprenticeship and apply to the bus garage as a backup. I'd keep every safe line shift I can get. In 2029 I'd inspect the robot trial results, ask Jo which physical maintenance jobs remain, and seek temporary wage support if our hours start falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed, even though I'd be busy doing something. I could learn a different machine, but there may be fewer places to be paid for learning it. Lena and I would feel each missing shift immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use your AI experience to move into dispatch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the screen, but full thinking AI can run dispatch itself in this picture. I don't want to build our whole plan on a desk that may be emptied first. The bus garage is hands-on, though I know its machines may change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a lost shift mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone replacing the refrigerator and pay the rent first. Lena's room-cleaning shifts rise and fall, so I can't put an exact number on the gap today. I'd tell our grown son not to send us money; he has his own household.

say: I would urge apprentices to inspect **trial equipment** before staffing decisions are made.
I would remind colleagues that **2031 AI** and 2034 robots affect different tasks.
think: I expect to need a **wage at 63** and perhaps at 66 too.
I see **physical maintenance** as possible work, while accepting some garage tasks will automate.
do: Request a **paid truck rotation** and funded maintenance course if offered.
Apply for **workshop posts** in 2032 and review household bills quarterly.
feel: Tense, but **five years** offers time to test actual job openings.
S3.quote: Retirement is near on a calendar, but our account isn't ready.
fieldNote: He translates the extra years into a **paid rotation** and asks which workshop tasks still need hands.
His **course condition** is explicit: employer funding, because he will not borrow against a thin household buffer.

steps.text: Request one paid truck-servicing rotation day each month
Take an accredited maintenance course if the utility funds it
Keep taking line shifts while training
Apply for paid workshop posts in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a five-year warning is worth using, not just talking about. In 2031 the office may lose thinking tasks, and around 2034 the robots may take many repairs. I'd want every apprentice to see the company's trial equipment before the staffing decision is made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 when AGI arrives, I'll still probably need a wage; at 66 when robots arrive, I might need one then too. Retirement is near on a calendar, but our account isn't ready. Five years might let me build maintenance experience, though the garage could automate parts of its work as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the utility to rotate me through truck servicing one day a month, on paid time, starting next spring. I'd take the accredited vehicle-maintenance course if the company funds it and keep line shifts for income. In 2032 I'd apply for paid workshop posts and ask Lena to review our bills with me every three months, so we know what wage we actually need before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one feels tense but workable. A rota and a course take time, yet I can start while my pay still comes in. I don't want to discover at 66 that I studied the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask during that truck rotation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mechanic which repairs are still done by hand and which diagnostic jobs have become software. I want to learn brakes and physical inspections, not only enter fault codes. I'd write down the jobs they actually hire for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you avoid studying the wrong thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every few months I'd check vacancies rather than trust a course brochure. If the utility doesn't fund the certificate, I wouldn't take a loan for it. I would still ask for the paid rotation and apply where I meet the requirements.

say: I would urge younger lineworkers to test **new roles** well before 2036.
I would distinguish **2036 office changes** from field robots around 2039.
think: I may still need **part-time wages** at 68, even with retirement near today.
I worry that **Lena's back** may limit her hotel work before my line job ends.
do: Transfer a **small payday amount** into an emergency account and adjust when hotel hours dip.
Keep **line shifts**, seek workshop sign-off, and review part-time work in 2037.
feel: More able to breathe, but uneasy about **ageing bodies** and uncertain future wages.
S4.quote: I hope I won't still be on a pole, but hope isn't income.
fieldNote: Colin's longer horizon supports **saving and supervised repairs**, not a promise that a pension will cover two people.
He keeps his son's **mortgage and children** outside the household plan, while allowing an honest family budget conversation.

steps.text: Transfer a small amount from each payday into the emergency account
Complete paid truck rotations and get workshop sign-off on physical repairs
Keep taking safe line shifts while they are available
Apply for part-time hands-on workshop work in 2037 if wages remain necessary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets us test a plan against actual pay and vacancies. Full thinking AI in 2036 would change our scheduling and records, then robots around 2039 would change the line itself. I wouldn't tell a young lineworker to wait until the last year to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 68 at the AI date and 71 at the robot date. I hope I won't still be on a pole, but hope isn't income. Lena will also be older, and hotel cleaning may be too much for her before then. A decade could let us save, change roles, and decide when to stop climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a small automatic transfer into our emergency account from every payday, starting now, and review it when Lena's hours dip. I'd try the paid truck rotation, keep line shifts, and apply for a workshop post once I've done enough supervised repairs. In 2037 I'd compare our actual income with our bills and take part-time hands-on work if we still need it, rather than assume we can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This picture gives me room to breathe, though I still feel a weight about Lena's back and my knees. I like having time to test the workshop route. The future wages are uncertain, so I wouldn't call us safe yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as enough supervised repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the workshop supervisor to sign off on brake checks and tool maintenance, not just tell me I looked keen. Then I could apply with something real on paper. If no post exists, I'd keep earning on the line as long as it's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown son to help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. He has two children and a mortgage of his own. I'd share our budget with him so there are no surprises, but Lena and I need to plan on our own wages and savings. I wouldn't count a possible pension amount until we get the statement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the office changes before we've saved anything and the line may follow three years later. A paid maintenance place and a clear company timetable would help. If shifts vanish, temporary wage support would keep our rent paid while I look for other hands-on work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays while an older worker learns a second trade. I will study after a shift, but I can't stop earning to become a trainee again. A training offer with no wage attached is a door I can't afford to walk through.

headlineQuote: A training offer with no wage attached is a door I can't afford to walk through.
portrait: Colin is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who entered the trade after delivery work and still studies equipment names.
He uses an **AI assistant daily**, then checks its answers against a printed manual and the physical part.
His and Lena's **thin savings** make continued paid shifts essential while her hotel hours fluctuate.
He explores **vehicle maintenance** through supervised repairs, funded training and real openings, without assuming retirement income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little time to build savings before line robots could shrink his crew in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid maintenance place**, a company timetable and temporary wage support would keep training possible without losing rent money.
